Subject: Post-demo: international fit briefing and L10N risk register

Thanks again for taking the time today — appreciated the candid discussion about EU/APAC regulatory requirements and the patient-data handling constraints for your regional deployments. Short recap and next steps below.

Key takeaways from the call:
- Primary use case: clinical triage assistance in German and Japanese front-ends (low-latency, high-precision NER + short summaries).
- Success metrics: F1 > 0.87 on named-entity extraction for German medical terms; summary hallucination rate < 3% on clinical vignette benchmark.
- Constraints: on-premise deployment for EU region (data residency), strict retention windows, SOC2 evidence required.

Immediate asks / next steps (mutual action plan):
1) We’ll deliver: recommended model shortlist + prompt sets tailored for DE/JA, a small benchmark pack, and an estimated cost/latency matrix (by 11/16). Attachment: prompt_set_v1.txt (starter), eurohealth_benchmark_links.md (drive links).
2) You: confirm the list of production locales (DE/JA + EN for fallback) and provide a sample PII-redacted dataset slice (~200 records) we can run an initial pass on by 11/20.
3) We’ll schedule a 30-min technical run-through with your infra lead to validate on-prem packaging constraints (suggested window: week of 11/20).

Preliminary model recommendations (quick view):
- For DE/EN: gpt-open-7B-q4 (low-latency quantized candidate), redwood-llama-13b-fp16 (higher-quality fallback)
- For JA: redwood-multilang-8B, with tokenizer optimizations for CJK sequences

Notes on risks we flagged: quantization can reduce tokenization fidelity for complex medical terms in German compounds; Japanese short-summary fluency may require language-pair-specific prompt engineering.

I’ve CC’d Neha (technical lead on model fit) so she can attach the shortlist and a small evaluation plan.

Thanks —

Thanks Vanessa — dug into the benchmark and sketched a recommended approach. High-level shortlist and rationale below; I attached a spreadsheet (neha_model_shortlist.xlsx) with latency simulations, expected token costs, and suggested quant configs.

Model shortlist (prioritized):
- gpt-open-7B-q4 (primary candidate for DE summarization): quantized q4_0 gives strong latency gains; estimated 95p latency ~340ms at 28 tokens on a single A10G equivalent instance with continuous batching. Main risk: tokenization edge-cases for long German compounds — add targeted tokenization exceptions and validation checks.
- redwood-llama-13b-fp16 (fallback for complex NER): higher quality, expected 95p ~720ms but much higher recall on nested medical entities. Use for asynchronous heavier tasks or as a canary fallback.
- redwood-multilang-8B (JA): balanced latency/quality; recommend q5 quant for CPU offload in the Private package if memory constrained.

Prompt and evaluation notes:
- Prompt set changes: add an explicit NER instruction block with examples of German compounds and preferred canonical spans; encourage conservative summarization (max 2 sentences) with a strict hallucination-check step (return "UNSURE" when confidence < threshold).
- Benchmarks: I linked a small synthetic set and our internal DE medical term list in eurohealth_benchmark_links.md; run both unit tests (NER F1) and downstream summary-accuracy checks.

Observability / regression gates (first 2 weeks):
- NER F1 per-entity-type tracked daily (alert if drop > 3 pts).
- Hallucination audit sampled (10/day) for clinical vignettes; escalate if >3% failures.
- Latency p95 and queue-length per route (alert if p95 > 450ms or queue-length > 12).

Compliance/ops notes:
- Private package supports KMS key wrapping in our EU region — ops can provide the KMS integration doc. But we need procurement to sign the Private SLA addendum (I can attach).

Attachments: neha_model_shortlist.xlsx (model simulations), eurohealth_benchmark_links.md (bench indexes), prompt_set_v1.txt (starter prompts)

—Neha
